claim: In female mice, mating creates a long-lasting sensory memory for the pheromones of the stud male that alters neuroendocrine responses to his chemosignals for many weeks.
source: In female mice, mating creates a long-lasting sensory memory for the pheromones of the stud male that alters neuroendocrine responses to his chemosignals for many weeks.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature on pheromonal learning in female mice.

claim: Imprinting led to striking plasticity in the intrinsic membrane excitability of projection neurons (mitral cells, MCs) that dramatically curtailed their responsiveness.
source: Imprinting led to striking plasticity in the intrinsic membrane excitability of projection neurons (mitral cells, MCs) that dramatically curtailed their responsiveness, suggesting a novel cellular substrate for pheromonal learning.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing changes in MC excitability after mating.

claim: Plasticity was selectively expressed in the MC ensembles activated by the stud male, consistent with formation of memories for specific individuals.
source: Plasticity was selectively expressed in the MC ensembles activated by the stud male, consistent with formation of memories for specific individuals.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data using fluorescent reporters to identify and record from stud-activated neurons.

claim: MC excitability gained atypical activity-dependence whose slow dynamics strongly attenuated firing on timescales of several minutes.
source: Finally, MC excitability gained atypical activity-dependence whose slow dynamics strongly attenuated firing on timescales of several minutes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing progressive reduction in MC firing over repeated stimulation trials.

claim: Chemical cues detected by the vomeronasal system convey vital social information, influencing diverse behaviors such as reproduction, pair bonding, parental care, individual recognition, and aggression.
source: Chemical cues detected by the vomeronasal system convey vital social information, influencing diverse behaviors such as reproduction (Bruce and Parrott, 1960; Kimchi et al., 2007), pair bonding (Young and Wang, 2004), parental care (Dulac et al., 2014; Kendrick et al., 1992; Lévy et al., 2004), individual recognition (Hurst, 2009), and aggression (Chamero et al., 2007; Stowers et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research on vomeronasal system functions.

claim: Vomeronasal pathways directly access the limbic system, consistent with their powerful role in guiding behavior.
source: Vomeronasal pathways directly access the limbic system, consistent with their powerful role in guiding behavior, and also influence neuroendocrine centers to modify physiological and hormonal status (Dulac and Torello, 2003; Tirindelli et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to anatomical and functional studies of vomeronasal pathways.

claim: During the first few days after fertilization, chemosignals from unfamiliar males typically block pregnancy by altering the female's neuroendocrine state.
source: During the first few days after fertilization, chemosignals from unfamiliar males typically block pregnancy by altering the female's neuroendocrine state (Bruce and Parrott, 1960).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the Bruce effect literature.

claim: Mating opens a plasticity window that creates a recognition memory for the stud's pheromones, so that they lose their potency and no longer disrupt embryo implantation.
source: However, mating opens a plasticity window that creates a recognition memory for the stud's pheromones, so that they lose their potency and no longer disrupt embryo implantation (Brennan and Keverne, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research on pheromonal imprinting.

claim: Memories are formed within hours, yet last weeks or longer.
source: Memories are formed within hours, yet last weeks or longer (Kaba and Keverne, 1988).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research on the duration of pheromonal memories.

claim: Mating-dependent learning is strongly linked to plasticity in the accessory olfactory bulb (AOB).
source: While social experience acts on diverse neural circuits throughout the brain (Wallace et al., 2009; Wu et al., 2014), mating-dependent learning is strongly linked to plasticity in the accessory olfactory bulb (AOB).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research and is further elaborated with specific evidence in subsequent sentences.

claim: Imprinting in females leads to local neurochemical changes.
source: Imprinting in females leads to local neurochemical changes (Brennan et al., 1995), is affected by local lesions or pharmacological interventions (Brennan and Keverne, 1997; Kaba et al., 1994; Kaba and Keverne, 1988), and can be artificially induced by manipulating AOB signaling (Kaba et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior experimental studies.

claim: Pheromonal cues are encoded in AOB by the firing of mitral cells (MCs), whose activity signals gender, hormonal status, and in particular, strain and/or individual identity.
source: Pheromonal cues are encoded in AOB by the firing of mitral cells (MCs), whose activity signals gender, hormonal status, and in particular, strain and/or individual identity (Ben-Shaul et al., 2010; Luo et al., 2003; Tolokh et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior electrophysiological studies of MC activity.

claim: Learning selectively suppresses the firing of the MCs encoding the stud male so that his pheromones no longer drive neuroendocrine responses, precluding pregnancy block.
source: Well-established theories propose that learning selectively suppresses the firing of the MCs encoding the stud male so that his pheromones no longer drive neuroendocrine responses, precluding pregnancy block (Brennan, 2004; Brennan et al., 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical models of pheromonal learning.

claim: MC suppression is proposed to depend on strengthening of local inhibitory circuits in AOB, consisting largely of granule cells (GCs) that supply feedback inhibition to MCs through unique dendrodendritic synapses.
source: MC suppression is further proposed to depend on strengthening of local inhibitory circuits in AOB, consisting largely of granule cells (GCs) that supply feedback inhibition to MCs through unique dendrodendritic synapses (Isaacson and Strowbridge, 1998; Shepherd and Greer, 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on AOB circuitry and proposed mechanisms of learning.

claim: Inhibitory plasticity is consistent with both microdialysis data and ultrastructural changes in local interneurons.
source: Inhibitory plasticity is consistent with both microdialysis data (Brennan and Binns, 2005; Brennan et al., 1995) and ultrastructural changes in local interneurons (Matsuoka et al., 1997, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior experimental studies.

claim: Direct measurements of either synaptic plasticity or changes in MC output are lacking.
source: To date, direct measurements of either synaptic plasticity or changes in MC output are lacking.
evidence: This claim identifies a gap in the literature based on the authors' knowledge of the field.

claim: There are no data linking plasticity to functionally defined cell populations.
source: Furthermore, while the selectivity of recognition memories for different individual or strains is thought to rely on changes in specific groups of MC, there are no data linking plasticity to functionally defined cell populations.
evidence: This claim identifies a gap in the literature based on the authors' knowledge of the field.

claim: Brief, high-frequency spike trains generated only modest feedback inhibition in AOB, comparable but smaller on average than reported in main olfactory bulb.
source: Brief, high-frequency spike trains generated only modest feedback inhibition in AOB (Figure 1B–C), comparable but smaller on average than reported in main olfactory bulb (Abraham et al., 2010; Margrie et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B-C and comparison to cited literature.

claim: Extended MC spike trains elicited slowly emerging but robust barrages of inhibitory postsynaptic potentials (IPSPs) that contributed to a strong decline in firing rate.
source: Extended MC spike trains elicited slowly emerging but robust barrages of inhibitory postsynaptic potentials (IPSPs) that contributed to a strong decline in firing rate (Figure 1D–1F; Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D-F.

claim: The same protocol generated little detectable inhibition in MCs of the main olfactory bulb, where high firing rates were sustained throughout the train.
source: In contrast, the same protocol generated little detectable inhibition in MCs of the main olfactory bulb, where high firing rates were sustained throughout the train.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing AOB and MOB responses.

claim: Pharmacologically eliminating feedback inhibition typically increased MC firing.
source: Pharmacologically eliminating feedback inhibition typically increased MC firing as well (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: MC self-inhibition is substantially stronger in AOB than in main olfactory bulb, but also unusually slow to manifest.
source: Together, our results suggest that MC self-inhibition is substantially stronger in AOB than in main olfactory bulb, but also unusually slow to manifest, consistent with the prolonged sensory responses characteristic of this brain area.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data comparing AOB and MOB responses.

claim: Powerful self-inhibition by single MCs could potentially provide a basis for cell-specific control over AOB output.
source: Such powerful self-inhibition by single MCs could potentially provide a basis for cell-specific control over AOB output, as previously proposed (Brennan and Keverne, 1997).
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from the data and prior theoretical proposals.

claim: Females engaged in frequent, repetitive investigation of males, particularly of facial and anogenital regions.
source: Females engaged in frequent, repetitive investigation of males, particularly of facial and anogenital regions (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C; mean interval, 62.1 ± 7.99 s; median, 15.9 s).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from video analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Investigative behavior was elevated in mated relative to sensory-exposed females.
source: Investigative behavior was elevated in mated relative to sensory-exposed females, suggesting that they experienced both heightened arousal states and increased levels of sensory input during the pairing period (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Mating substantially increases mIPSC frequency in mitral cells.
source: The frequency of mIPSCs was strongly increased in mated animals vs. naïve and sensory-exposed groups (Figure 2C–D; 2.45 ± 0.37 Hz vs. 1.48 ± 0.21 Hz and 1.28 ± 0.17 Hz respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: The mean amplitude of mIPSCs was similar for all three conditions (naïve, sensory-exposed, and mated).
source: The mean amplitude of mIPSCs was similar for all three conditions, suggesting little change in the postsynaptic sensitivity of inhibitory synapses onto MCs (Figure 2E–F; 56.8 ± 3.5 pA, 54.5 ± 3.8 pA, and 65.8 ± 6.1 pA for naïve, sensory-exposed and mated mice respectively; Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E-F.

claim: Mating increased inhibitory input onto MCs, consistent with prior microdialysis results.
source: Overall, mating experience substantially increased inhibitory input onto MCs, consistent with prior microdialysis results (Brennan et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and comparison to cited literature.

claim: The frequency of sEPSPs in granule cells was elevated in mated relative to naïve and sensory-exposed females.
source: The frequency of sEPSPs was elevated in mated relative to naïve and sensory-exposed females (Figure 2H–I; 4.25 ± 0.71, 3.57 ± 0.56, and 6.61 ± 0.63 Hz for naïve, exposure and mated groups respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2H-I.

claim: EPSP amplitude in granule cells was slightly enhanced in mated compared to naïve animals.
source: EPSP amplitude was also slightly enhanced in mated compared to naïve animals (Figure 2J–K, 1.08 ± 0.08, 1.18 ± 0.10, and 1.44 ± 0.10 mV for naïve, exposed, and mated groups respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2J-K.

claim: Imprinting upregulates both the excitatory and inhibitory components of the pathways for MC self-inhibition.
source: Together, our data suggest that imprinting upregulates both the excitatory and inhibitory components of the pathways for MC self-inhibition.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined experimental data on inhibitory and excitatory synaptic changes.

claim: Mating combined with subsequent sensory exposure drove strong GFP expression in a subset of GCs in Arc-GFP animals.
source: However, mating combined with subsequent sensory exposure drove strong GFP expression in a subset of GCs, consistent with Arc immunolabeling in AOB in response to conspecifics (Halem et al., 2001; Matsuoka et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and comparison to cited literature.

claim: Robust labeling was found in both anterior and posterior AOB, in agreement with prior reports using histochemical staining.
source: We found robust labeling in both anterior and posterior AOB, in agreement with prior reports using histochemical staining (Brennan et al., 1992; Halem et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations and comparison to cited literature.

claim: Mean amplitude and frequency of sEPSPs are similar for GFP(-) and GFP(+) GCs in mated mice.
source: Unexpectedly, there was no difference between GFP(-) and GFP(+) populations of GCs for either amplitude or frequency of spontaneous excitatory input (Figure 3C–D; amplitude, 1.43 ± 0.15 vs 1.48 ± 0.13 mV; frequency, 7.13 ± 0.98 vs. 6.41 ± 0.84 Hz for unlabeled and labeled cells respectively; Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C-D.

claim: There was no significant relationship between the intensity of GFP expression and either amplitude or frequency of EPSPs in granule cells.
source: Similarly, there was no significant relationship between the intensity of GFP expression and either amplitude or frequency of EPSPs (Figure 3E–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E-F.

claim: Mating globally increased synaptic drive onto inhibitory GCs without apparent specificity to the neurons activated by the stud male.
source: These data suggest that mating globally increased synaptic drive onto inhibitory GCs without apparent specificity to the neurons activated by the stud male.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing no difference between GFP(+) and GFP(-) populations.

claim: Fos-GFP levels were low in MCs from naïve females, but were robustly elevated in a subset of MCs after mating.
source: Fos-GFP levels were low in MCs from naïve females, but were robustly elevated in a subset of MCs after mating (Figure 3G; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: There was no significant difference in mean amplitude and frequency of mIPSCs between GFP(-) and GFP(+) MCs in mated females.
source: Similar to interneuron results, there was no significant difference in mean amplitude and frequency of mIPSCs between GFP(-) and GFP(+) MCs (Figure 3I and J; amplitude, 65.98 ± 8.15 vs. 57.86 ± 3.15 pA for unlabeled and labeled cells respectively; frequency, 1.43 ± 0.18 vs. 1.83 ± 0.31 Hz).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3I-J.

claim: There was no apparent correlation between GFP levels and properties of mIPSCs in mitral cells.
source: Furthermore, there was no apparent correlation between GFP levels and properties of mIPSCs (Figure 3K and L).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3K-L.

claim: Imprinting drives synaptic plasticity in AOB inhibitory circuits, but synaptic changes were widely distributed across both GC and MC populations with no apparent relationship to activation during mating.
source: Together, these results further indicate that imprinting drives synaptic plasticity in AOB inhibitory circuits. In contrast with established learning models, however, synaptic changes were widely distributed across both GC and MC populations with no apparent relationship to activation during mating.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined experimental data on synaptic changes in different cell populations.

claim: The responsiveness of GCs in Arc-GFP females was enhanced after mating, so that less current was needed to initiate firing, and higher firing rates were produced by the same current steps.
source: The responsiveness of GCs in Arc-GFP females was enhanced after mating, so that less current was needed to initiate firing, and higher firing rates were produced by the same current steps (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: GC resting potentials were consistently depolarized in mated versus naïve animals.
source: Increased excitability was also reflected in GC resting potentials, which were consistently depolarized in mated versus naïve animals (Figure 4C, −72.1 ± 1.6, –71.0 ± 1.6, and −66.3 ± 1.2 mV for naïve, exposed, and mated groups respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Membrane resistance and slope of the input-output firing function were unchanged across groups in granule cells.
source: Other properties, such as membrane resistance and slope of the input-output firing function, were unchanged across groups (Figure 4D, Rinput = 469 ± 35 vs. 520 ± 34 for naïve and mated groups; p=0.31; ANOVA with post-hoc Tukey test), suggesting that increased GC responsiveness was largely determined by resting potential.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Mating increased the intrinsic excitability of AOB interneurons.
source: Overall, mating increased the intrinsic excitability of AOB interneurons, suggesting that synaptic plasticity in inhibitory circuits is complemented by additional non-synaptic mechanisms.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data on GC excitability changes.

claim: GC resting potential was uncorrelated with intensity of Arc-GFP labeling in both sensory-exposed and mated animals.
source: As with synaptic measurements, GC resting potential was uncorrelated with GFP intensity (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Mean resting potential was similar for GFP(-) and GFP(+) GC populations in mated animals.
source: Furthermore, when we subdivided the GC dataset from mated animals into GFP(-) and GFP(+) populations, mean resting potential was similar for the two groups (Figure 4F; −67.0 ± 2.2 vs. −65.4 ± 1.9 mV respectively; Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Intrinsic plasticity in granule cells was widespread across interneurons, and lacked dependence on prior activation during mating.
source: Together, the increased GC excitability after mating indicates that learning acts on intrinsic as well as synaptic properties of AOB neurons. However, intrinsic plasticity was widespread across interneurons, and lacked dependence on prior activation during mating.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing no correlation between GFP labeling and resting potential.

claim: Mating had no apparent effect on MC responses to a single stimulus.
source: In contrast to GCs, however, mating had no apparent effect on MC responses to a single stimulus.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing MC responses in naïve and mated animals.

claim: There was no difference in peak firing rate, total spike count during the train, or decay of firing between naïve and mated females for a single MC stimulus.
source: We found no difference in peak firing rate, total spike count during the train, or decay of firing between naïve and mated females (Figure 5B–D; peak firing: 15.0 ± 3.0 Hz vs. 17.4 ± 1.8 Hz; total spike count: 153 ± 28 vs. 176 ± 25 for naïve vs. mated respectively; Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B-D.

claim: In mated females, MC firing often declined dramatically across successive trials during repetitive stimulation.
source: Surprisingly, in mated females MC firing often declined dramatically across successive trials, so that even neurons initially responding with hundreds of action potentials ceased firing entirely (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: MC attenuation was greatly enhanced after imprinting, so that average spike counts in mated females dropped to less than half than that of controls.
source: While firing also declined in some neurons from naïve animals, MC attenuation was greatly enhanced after imprinting, so that average spike counts in mated females dropped to less than half than that of controls (Figure 5F–G; 80 ± 11% vs. 36 ± 8%).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F-G.

claim: Mating leads to an unusual form of plasticity in MC membrane properties, where firing gains a striking dependence on recent history of activity.
source: Together, our data indicate that mating leads to an unusual form of plasticity in MC membrane properties, where firing gains a striking dependence on recent history of activity.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data on MC responses to repetitive stimulation.

claim: Metaplasticity in intrinsic excitability dramatically suppresses MC firing to repetitive stimuli and curtails their responsiveness on timescales of minutes.
source: This metaplasticity in intrinsic excitability offers an alternative mechanism for attenuating AOB output, dramatically suppressing MC firing to repetitive stimuli and curtailing their responsiveness on timescales of minutes.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data and represents an interpretation of the functional significance.

claim: Mating drove robust increases in Fos-GFP relative to sensory-exposed controls, generating detectable labeling in approximately 25% of MCs.
source: Mating drove robust increases in Fos-GFP relative to sensory-exposed controls, generating detectable labeling in approximately 25% of MCs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: After mating, both labeled and unlabeled MCs fired similarly to initial stimuli.
source: After mating, both labeled and unlabeled MCs fired similarly to initial stimuli, consistent with responses in Arc-GFP mice (Figure 6A–D; peak firing rate, 15.2 ± 3.2 Hz vs. 16.2 ± 2.4 Hz; total spike count, 155 ± 39 vs. 133 ± 26 for GFP(-) and GFP(+) respectively; Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A-D.

claim: In unlabeled MCs, firing was stable across trials, or even increased slightly over time.
source: In unlabeled MCs, firing was stable across trials, or even increased slightly over time (Figure 6E–F; spike count of 10th vs. 1st trial, 115 ± 17%, peak firing rate, 87.0 ± 11.4%).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E-F.

claim: The output of GFP(+) MCs decreased markedly over successive stimuli.
source: In contrast, the output of GFP(+) MCs decreased markedly over successive stimuli (Figure 6F–H; spike count of 10th vs. 1st trial, 30.7 ± 12.3%; peak firing, 29.4 ± 10.2%).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F-H.

claim: Reduced excitability arises specifically in the MC ensemble activated by the stud during mating and subsequent sensory experience.
source: These data indicate that reduced excitability arises specifically in the MC ensemble activated by the stud during mating and subsequent sensory experience.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data comparing GFP(+) and GFP(-) MC populations.

claim: In the absence of mating, both GFP(+) and GFP(-) MC populations maintained consistent firing over all trials.
source: In contrast to results in mated females, however, both GFP(-) and GFP(+) populations maintained consistent firing over all trials, despite their differences in initial responsiveness (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D-F.

claim: Dynamic changes in MC excitability result from imprinting, and emerge specifically in the population labeled during mating.
source: These data further indicate that dynamic changes in MC excitability result from imprinting, and emerge specifically in the population labeled during mating.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data comparing mated and sensory-exposed animals.

claim: MC suppression was intact even after eliminating local circuit interactions, indicating that it did not depend on persistent inhibition.
source: MC suppression was intact even after eliminating local circuit interactions, indicating that it did not depend on persistent inhibition (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Repeated stimulation led to a progressive hyperpolarization of MC membrane potential in mated females.
source: We further probed the source of reduced MC firing by examining membrane properties over the course of stimulus trains. Repeated stimulation led to a progressive hyperpolarization of MC membrane potential, both in randomly selected MCs in mated Arc-GFP females (Figure 7A) and in GFP(+) MCs in mated Fos-GFP mice (Figure 7B; Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A-B.

claim: Initial MC resting potential was indistinguishable between naïve and mated females in Arc-GFP mice.
source: These changes were not predicted by initial MC resting potential, which was indistinguishable between naïve and mated females in Arc-GFP mice (Figure 7C; −58.0 ± 1.1 mV vs. −56.7 ± 0.7 mV respectively), and between GFP(+) and GFP(-) populations within mated Fos-GFP females (Figure 7C; −55.0 ± 1.5 vs. −53.9 ± 1.1 mV, p=0.56, t-test; n = 7 and 11 respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: GFP(+) MCs were hyperpolarized by −3.3 ± 0.5 mV vs. 0.2 ± 0.6 for GFP(-) neurons on average.
source: On average, GFP(+) MCs were hyperpolarized by −3.3 ± 0.5 mV vs. 0.2 ± 0.6 for GFP(-) neurons (Figure 7D; p<0.05, t-test).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: MC hyperpolarization was strongly correlated with loss of firing.
source: MC hyperpolarization was strongly correlated with loss of firing (Figure 7E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Reduced MC output is due to changes in intrinsic membrane properties rather than altered synaptic inhibition.
source: Together, these data further indicate that reduced MC output is due to changes in intrinsic membrane properties rather than altered synaptic inhibition, imparting stud-activated neurons with a sensitivity to recent firing that progressively dampens their output.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data on MC hyperpolarization and pharmacological experiments.

claim: Each firing bout led to hyperpolarization that decayed extremely slowly, lasting until the onset of the next stimulus.
source: To further probe the time course of plasticity, we probed randomly selected MCs in mated females using stimuli spaced 2 min and 3 min apart. Each firing bout led to hyperpolarization that decayed extremely slowly, lasting until the onset of the next stimulus (Figure 7G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7G.

claim: Intervals of both 2 min and 3 min gave comparable levels of hyperpolarization and attenuated firing after 10 stimuli.
source: Intervals of both 2 min and 3 min gave comparable levels of hyperpolarization and attenuated firing after 10 stimuli (Figure 7G–H; mean ∆Vm, −5.64 ± 0.88 and −6.02 ± 2.05 mV for 2 and 3 min intervals respectively; normalized spike count, 0.176 ± 0.116 and 0.193 ± 0.089 for 2 and 3 min).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7G-H.

claim: MC suppression lasted for total periods of an hour or longer.
source: When possible, we tested MCs again at 15 min and 35 min after the offset of stimulation, which revealed that suppression lasted for total periods of an hour or longer (normalized spike count, 0.149 ± 0.080 and 0.117 ± 0.072 at 15 and 35 min respectively; ∆Vm, −5.85 ± 1.49 and −6.21 ± 1.97 at 15 and 35 min).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from extended recording sessions.

claim: MC plasticity persists on the timescales relevant to physiology and behavior in vivo.
source: These results indicate that MC plasticity persists on the timescales relevant to physiology and behavior in vivo.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data on the duration of MC suppression.

claim: The study provides the first direct measurements of the synaptic and cellular effects of pheromonal learning in females after mating.
source: Our data provide the first direct measurements of the synaptic and cellular effects of pheromonal learning in females after mating.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' knowledge of the literature and the novelty of their experimental approach.

claim: Synaptic plasticity lacked the specificity thought to be required for recognition memories.
source: However, using targeted measurements from identified mating-activated ensembles, we found that synaptic plasticity lacked the specificity thought to be required for recognition memories.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing no correlation between synaptic changes and GFP labeling.

claim: A striking reduction in intrinsic excitability in MCs suggests a novel basis for storing sensory experience in AOB.
source: Surprisingly, we also found a striking reduction in intrinsic excitability in MCs, suggesting a novel basis for storing sensory experience in AOB.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data on MC excitability changes and represents an interpretation of their significance.

claim: Loss of MC responsiveness was confined to the set of MCs activated during mating, consistent with a stud-selective recognition memory.
source: Notably, this loss of responsiveness was confined to the set of MCs activated during mating, consistent with a stud-selective recognition memory.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data comparing GFP(+) and GFP(-) MC populations.

claim: MC output was initially unchanged after mating, but instead progressively decreased depending on recent activity.
source: MC excitability also showed unusual dynamics, where output was initially unchanged, but instead progressively decreased depending on recent activity.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data on MC responses to repetitive stimulation.

claim: Slow MC dynamics may selectively filter repetitive vomeronasal inputs over extended timescales, preserving sensitivity at the onset of behavioral encounters while reducing their longer-term impact on neuroendocrine centers.
source: Slow MC dynamics may selectively filter repetitive vomeronasal inputs over extended timescales, preserving sensitivity at the onset of behavioral encounters while reducing their longer-term impact on neuroendocrine centers that control hormonal status and pregnancy.
evidence: This claim is speculative, representing a proposed functional interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: The data are broadly consistent with the selective MC plasticity proposed by existing learning models, but also suggest a new and unanticipated cellular mechanism that complements changes in synaptic strength.
source: Our data are broadly consistent with the selective MC plasticity proposed by existing learning models, but also suggest a new and unanticipated cellular mechanism that complements changes in synaptic strength.
evidence: This claim represents an interpretation of how the findings relate to existing theoretical models.

claim: Self-inhibition in AOB emerged surprisingly slowly, building over several seconds so that it was strongest during prolonged MC firing on the timescales of natural sensory-evoked responses.
source: Self-inhibition in AOB also emerged surprisingly slowly, building over several seconds so that it was strongest during prolonged MC firing on the timescales of natural sensory-evoked responses (Ben-Shaul et al., 2010; Luo et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and comparison to cited literature on sensory response timescales.

claim: The basis for differences in self-inhibition in AOB and MOB are unclear, but may be linked to the prominent role of mGluRs in AOB.
source: The basis for differences in self-inhibition in AOB and MOB are unclear, but may be linked to the prominent role of mGluRs in AOB (Castro et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing a potential mechanism based on cited literature.

claim: Increased frequency of excitatory input to GCs implies upregulation of release sites in MC dendrites.
source: Increased frequency of excitatory input to GCs implies upregulation of release sites in MC dendrites, and enhanced amplitude suggests strengthening of postsynaptic contacts, consistent with the ultrastructural enlargements seen in the postsynaptic density (Ichikawa, 2003; Matsuoka et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data and comparison to cited ultrastructural studies.

claim: Increased frequency of mIPSCs in MCs suggests enhanced release of GABA from GCs, which could result either from changes in existing contacts or addition of new synapses via spine growth or recruitment of adult-born interneurons.
source: Increased frequency of mIPSCs in MCs also suggests enhanced release of GABA from GCs, which could result either from changes in existing contacts or addition of new synapses via spine growth or recruitment of adult-born interneurons (Mak and Weiss, 2010; Shingo et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data and proposes potential mechanisms based on cited literature.

claim: Increased release of GABA may be counterbalanced by short-term dynamics during extended firing.
source: Increased release of GABA may be counterbalanced by short-term dynamics during extended firing (Dietz and Murthy, 2005), or alternatively changes in mIPSCs may reflect top-down inputs to AOB (Fan and Luo, 2009) that would contribute to spontaneous but not recurrent inhibition.
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing potential explanations for the observed data based on cited literature.

claim: Non-specific plasticity runs counter to existing models of pheromonal learning.
source: While non-specific plasticity runs counter to existing models, our data do not exclude a role for inhibition in learning or sensory processing.
evidence: This claim represents an interpretation of how the findings relate to existing theoretical models.

claim: GABAergic circuits may be differentially recruited in vivo, where complex natural cues activate larger MC populations.
source: GABAergic circuits may be differentially recruited in vivo, where complex natural cues activate larger MC populations (Ben-Shaul et al., 2010; Meeks et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing a potential explanation based on cited literature.

claim: Inhibition strongly shapes MC firing in the intact brain.
source: Inhibition strongly shapes MC firing in the intact brain (Hendrickson et al., 2008), and descending pathways targeting AOB are likely to further shape sensory responses (Fan and Luo, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The nonspecific nature of inhibitory plasticity suggests it may act in concert with other, more targeted changes in the AOB circuit.
source: Overall, however, the nonspecific nature of inhibitory plasticity suggests it may act in concert with other, more targeted changes in the AOB circuit.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental findings and represents an interpretation of their functional significance.

claim: Experience-dependent changes in excitability often accompany synaptic modifications in both mammalian and invertebrate systems.
source: Experience-dependent changes in excitability often accompany synaptic modifications in both mammalian and invertebrate systems (Daoudal and Debanne, 2003; Zhang and Linden, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Altered intrinsic properties support homeostatic regulation in cortical circuits, scaling cellular excitability to match long-term changes in sensory input.
source: Altered intrinsic properties support homeostatic regulation in cortical circuits, scaling cellular excitability to match long-term changes in sensory input (Desai et al., 1999; Turrigiano, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Often, learning acts to enhance excitability, acting to amplify responses to trained sensory inputs, or to select neural populations encoding the learned cue.
source: Often, learning acts to enhance excitability (Barkai and Saar, 2001; Zhang and Linden, 2003), acting to amplify responses to trained sensory inputs (Mozzachiodi and Byrne, 2010), or to select neural populations encoding the learned cue (Yiu et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: MC excitability was strongly reduced by pheromonal learning, in contrast to other learning paradigms.
source: Here, in contrast, MC excitability was strongly reduced by pheromonal learning.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and represents a comparison to other learning systems.

claim: The sign reversal in excitability changes is consistent with the fact that imprinting leads to the suppression of an otherwise default neuroendocrine response to sensory input.
source: This sign reversal is consistent with the fact that imprinting leads to the suppression of an otherwise default neuroendocrine response to sensory input.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data and represents an interpretation of the functional significance.

claim: MC hyperpolarization accumulated after each trial and lasted for at least 30 min after the offset of stimulation.
source: MC hyperpolarization accumulated after each trial and lasted for at least 30 min after the offset of stimulation, suggesting that MCs display an unusual and highly integrative form of intrinsic membrane plasticity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and represents an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Membrane excitability offers a simple way to selectively control the output of specific MC populations, whereas inhibitory plasticity would need to be coordinated across large sets of GCs, and further targeted to the specific synapses onto stud-encoding MCs.
source: Membrane excitability offers a simple way to selectively control the output of specific MC populations, whereas inhibitory plasticity would need to be coordinated across large sets of GCs, and further targeted to the specific synapses onto stud-encoding MCs.
evidence: This claim represents a speculative interpretation of the potential advantages of intrinsic versus synaptic plasticity.

claim: Intrinsic excitability may be particularly well suited to mediating learning in dedicated sensory pathways coupled to stereotyped behavioral responses.
source: Intrinsic excitability may be particularly well suited to mediating learning in dedicated sensory pathways coupled to stereotyped behavioral responses.
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing a potential functional advantage of the observed mechanism.

claim: Learning does not cause simple, static changes in MC excitability per se, but instead leads to metaplastic effects that impart sensitivity to recent firing levels.
source: Thus, learning does not cause simple, static changes in MC excitability per se, but instead leads to metaplastic effects that impart sensitivity to recent firing levels.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data on MC responses to repetitive stimulation.

claim: Metaplasticity in the intrinsic excitability of MCs may rely on changes in composition of membrane conductances.
source: In metaplasticity of synaptic strength, experience shifts thresholds for potentiation and depression via changes in NMDA subunit composition (Abraham, 2008; Lee et al., 2010). Metaplasticity in the intrinsic excitability of MCs may rely on similar changes in composition of membrane conductances.
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing a potential mechanism based on analogy to synaptic metaplasticity.

claim: Prolonged hyperpolarization and lowered membrane resistance are consistent with changes in potassium channels such as HCN or Ca2+-dependent K+ currents.
source: Prolonged hyperpolarization and lowered membrane resistance are consistent with changes in potassium channels such as HCN or Ca2+-dependent K+ currents, which are present in main olfactory bulb and linked to learning in other systems (Lin et al., 2008; Nolan et al., 2004, 2003; Stackman et al., 2002; Wang et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing potential mechanisms based on the observed data and cited literature.

claim: MC firing is modulated by intrinsic conductances such as CAN currents, which boost synaptic responses.
source: MC firing is also modulated by intrinsic conductances such as CAN currents, which boost synaptic responses (Shpak et al., 2014, 2012) and likely contributed to accelerated firing rates seen over the first few seconds of stimulation in our study.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental observations and cited literature on MC conductances.

claim: AOB MCs express multiple activity-dependent conductances that dynamically modulate their firing depending on the strength, duration, and biological context of activity.
source: AOB MCs thus appear to express multiple activity-dependent conductances that dynamically modulate their firing depending on the strength, duration, and biological context of activity.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data and represents a synthesis of the findings.

claim: One potential role of dynamic, activity-dependent changes in excitability is to high-pass filter vomeronasal input, preserving responsiveness at the onset of social interactions while selectively attenuating the long-lasting, repetitive AOB activity required for neuroendocrine changes.
source: One potential role is to high-pass filter vomeronasal input, preserving responsiveness at the onset of social interactions for appropriate selection of aggressive, reproductive, or parental behaviors (Burns-Cusato et al., 2004; Clancy et al., 1984; Stowers et al., 2002; Tachikawa et al., 2013), while selectively attenuating the long-lasting, repetitive AOB activity required for the neuroendocrine changes that block pregnancy (Li et al., 1994; Rosser et al., 1989).
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing a potential functional role based on the experimental findings and cited literature.

claim: Slow activity dynamics may help reduce interference between memories of different individuals.
source: Similarly, slow activity dynamics may help reduce interference between memories of different individuals.
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing a potential functional advantage of the observed mechanism.

claim: Different males have similar chemical signatures, suggesting that they may also have overlapping neural representations in AOB.
source: Different males have similar chemical signatures (Harvey et al., 1989), suggesting that they may also have overlapping neural representations in AOB.
evidence: This claim is inferred from cited literature on chemical signatures and represents a logical inference about neural representations.

claim: Eliminating the responses of stud-encoding MCs could disrupt representations of other, non-imprinted animals.
source: Eliminating the responses of stud-encoding MCs could therefore also disrupt representations of other, non-imprinted animals.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the previous claim about overlapping representations.

claim: Delayed changes in MC output may help minimize the impact of plasticity on overlapping sensory codes.
source: Delayed changes in MC output may help minimize the impact of plasticity on overlapping sensory codes.
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing a potential functional advantage of the observed dynamics.

claim: The effects of mating on pregnancy block can last for many weeks.
source: The effects of mating on pregnancy block, however, can last for many weeks (Brennan et al., 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Sensory memories could be stored initially in AOB and then transferred to other areas, as seen in other memory systems.
source: Alternatively, sensory memories could be stored initially in AOB and then transferred to other areas, as seen in other memory systems (Preston and Eichenbaum, 2013; Ross and Eichenbaum, 2006).
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing an alternative explanation based on cited literature on memory systems.

claim: Many contexts where animals show flexibility in vomeronasal-guided behaviors involve the loss of an otherwise default response, similar to the effects of mating.
source: Interestingly, many of these involve the loss of an otherwise default response, similar to the effects of mating.
evidence: This claim is based on knowledge of vomeronasal-mediated behaviors and represents a comparison across different contexts.

claim: Males shift from attack to parental behaviors towards pups.
source: Males shift from attack to parental behaviors towards pups (Tachikawa et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2014), and regulate aggression towards other males to form dominance hierarchies (Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Behavioral responses to fear-inducing cues such as predator odors can habituate with repeated presentation.
source: Behavioral responses to fear-inducing cues such as predator odors can also habituate with repeated presentation (Takahashi et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: It is currently unclear whether the behavioral plasticity seen in other paradigms relies on similar cellular mechanisms in AOB.
source: It is currently unclear whether the behavioral plasticity seen in other paradigms relies on similar cellular mechanisms in AOB, and it will be important for future work to test this possibility.
evidence: This claim identifies a gap in knowledge and proposes a direction for future research.

claim: Changes in MC excitability could contribute to flexibility in other vomeronasal-mediated behaviors, which often involve suppression of otherwise default sensory responses.
source: Changes in MC excitability could also contribute to flexibility in other vomeronasal-mediated behaviors, which often involve suppression of otherwise default sensory responses (Tachikawa et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing a potential broader application of the findings based on cited literature.

claim: While the AOB is a critical node in the vomeronasal pathway, MC plasticity likely acts in parallel with broader changes across the extended network of brain regions that couple chemosensory input to behavior.
source: While the AOB is a critical node in the vomeronasal pathway, MC plasticity likely acts in parallel with broader changes across the extended network of brain regions that couple chemosensory input to behavior (Dulac et al., 2014; Wu et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is inferred from knowledge of vomeronasal circuitry and cited literature.
